newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Chinese Butterfly Ying Huang flies to Manhattan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Chinese Butterfly Ying Huang flies to Manhattan.

text.p: Chinese soprano Ying Huang, who scored a fairytale breakthrough when she was cast as the star of a film version of Puccini's "Madame Butterfly," has flown to Manhattan, hoping to launch an international career.

"New York, that's the best place for artists and musicians," said Huang, 28, speaking in lightly accented English, the result of a rigorous two-year study programme. "It's not easy to move to foreign country. Everything's difficult at the beginning, right? But it's very important, especially if I'm to become a Western-style musician."
She added disarmingly: "I'm not sure or confident with my English. I know I make mistakes but I want to communicate."

The Shanghai-born Huang learned English because "even in musical circles in Europe, whether I go to Italy or Germany or France, most people speak English. Most people are nice to correct my English. But I don't forget my Chinese anyway."

Sony Classical this month is releasing her first solo CD, mostly "bel canto" arias like those popularised by Maria Callas by composers such as Donizetti, Rossini, Verdi and Puccini. Huang also sings two Chinese songs, "I Live at the Source of the Chang Tang River" and "A Little Path." For the CD's Korean release, two Korean songs will be substituted.

Huang, delicate-looking and petite, modestly describes her voice as "delicate." That may be true, but she has the tireless work ethic of a stevedore. For her album, she spent months practicing with famed 1960s Metropolitan soprano Renata Scotto as her coach.
"It's terribly important to sing these in the proper style and the language," she explained. "That's why I needed a mentor like Renata. She's the specialist of 'bel canto.'"

Timed with the album's release is the American debut, on public television on July 2nd, of her filmed "Butterfly," which, like her CD, was conducted by James Conlon. Frederic Mitterrand, a nephew of the late French president, directed.

"It was an unusual chance," Huang said of her Cinderella-like "discovery" for the starring role in the film as a result of a videotape she sent from China to Paris. Most of opera's great divas have sung the role of Butterfly on stage, but Mitterrand had launched a worldwide talent search for an Oriental soprano who was young and attractive enough to play the doomed Japanese heroine convincingly in a film.
Huang, an unknown, was the right age and photogenic; although she is a "light" soprano, with proper coaching she could successfully manage the "heavy" dramatic role.

"I took quite a long time to accept he reality of that film because I thought it was like dream," Huang recalled. "Also this role was not good for my voice. I'm a very light lyric coloratura soprano and this role is for a dramatic soprano. I could not believe I could really sing this role."

"Fortunately, it was a movie, different completely from a real opera on the stage. There was a technique for singing in front of the microphone," she said, adding: "Maybe that's the only opera movie I could do in my whole life."

"After the movie, because people get to know me, I've gotten busy, especially this season," she said. "I will be performing a lot, particularly in America," where she will sing in Boston on July 21st and at the Lincoln Center's Mostly Mozart festival in New York on Aug. 13.
"I'm doing Mozart concert arias and a Mozart cantata which has never been performed with other singers. I'm just learning that now," she said.
